podcast.body: A seminal, groundbreaking rock and roll song released in October 1955. It was considered outrageously cool at the time, particularly for those aware of the original version's gay overtures in the lyrics, but too outrageous for much of white America. "In October 1955, Little Richard released this seminal groundbreaking rock and roll song."

podcast.body: During his wild 1962 UK tour performances, Little Richard famously faked his own death on stage, collapsing off the piano and lying still, only to suddenly jump up and launch into "Tutti Frutti," creating a dramatic effect and engaging the audience. "Just to create attention in the audience for when he suddenly jumped up and started singing Tuti Fruity."

podcast.body: Little Richard's legendary barnburner and "veiled sex anthem" from the 1950s, which cracked the pop charts and peaked at number seven. He is notable for having written the song himself, with a "sanitizing assist" from lyrics editor Dorothy LaBostrie. "Richard cracked the pop charts with his legendary Barnburner and veiled sex anthem, 2D Frudey."

The original, uncensored lyrics of "Tutti Frutti" are mentioned as containing not-so-subtle hints about his sexuality, specifically being gay or bisexual with gay leanings, when the song was written and released. "search for the original, uncensored lyrics of Tuti Fruity."

podcast.body: This song began as a sexually explicit R&B joke song with unbroadcastable lyrics ("A Wopper Bopper loom up a good god damn, Judy Fruity good booty, if it don't fit don't force it, you can grease it make it easy"). Bumps Blackwell realized its hit potential and had Dorothy LaBostrie rewrite the lyrics to be broadcastable and about a girl named Sue. Richard played piano on the track, which was cut in three takes, and it became a massive hit, reaching number 21 on the pop charts. "Tutti frutti was indeed a massive hit."
